title: Self-explainable Operator Learning for Discovering Spatial Patterns in Functional Data
authors: Mojgan Alishiri, Amirhossein Arzani
abstract: Operator learning has emerged as a powerful tool for modeling complex physical systems in functional spaces. However, their neural network-based architectures make them opaque models, obscuring the reasoning behind their predictions. In this work, we introduce a self-explainable operator learning framework that overcomes this challenge by reformulating operator learning as a linear combination of generalized functional linear models expressed through integral equations. Exploiting the additive decomposability of these integral equations, we divide the input domain into subdomains and compute localized integrals to evaluate the contribution of each region to the final prediction. This decomposition enables direct interpretability where the model explains both inputs and outputs by linking specific input regions to corresponding output patterns, thereby revealing which spatial features drive predictions. We demonstrate the framework on function-to-scalar and function-to-function mappings in fluid flow problems involving blood flow and unsteady aerodynamics. The results show that the operator most often prioritizes regions with strong feature gradients, providing physically meaningful insight into the model's decision-making process. Comparisons with established post-hoc explainability methods demonstrate qualitative agreement while highlighting the key advantage of the proposed approach: explainability is embedded directly within the operator structure itself and does not require an external tool. Therefore, our framework provides a mathematically transparent and physically interpretable approach to uncover relationships within data, fostering trust in machine learning for scientific applications by enabling more informed data-driven analysis of physical systems.

infographic.key_insight: The paper makes operator learning self-explainable by decomposing predictions into localized integral contributions, revealing which input regions drive each output pattern.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a transparent way to trust and diagnose data-driven models for fluid mechanics problems such as blood flow and unsteady aerodynamics.
method: Reformulate operator learning as a linear combination of generalized functional linear models.
Split the input domain into subdomains and compute localized integrals to measure regional importance.
Embed interpretability directly into the operator, avoiding separate post-hoc explainability tools.
infographic.evidence_signal: The framework is evaluated on function-to-scalar and function-to-function fluid-flow tasks, with explanations that align qualitatively with established post-hoc methods and often emphasize regions of strong feature gradients.
infographic.watch_item: Localization-based explanations may depend on how the domain is partitioned, so implementation choices could affect the granularity and stability of the interpreted regions.
infographic.paper_title: Self-explainable Operator Learning for Discovering Spatial Patterns in Functional Data

title: An Inner-Scaled Linear Contribution to Wall-Pressure Variance at High Reynolds Number
authors: J. M. O. Massey, S. J. Zimmerman, J. C. Klewicki, B. J. McKeon
abstract: In canonical turbulent wall-bounded flows, the inner-scaled wall-pressure variance is empirically well described by a constant offset plus a slope logarithmic in the friction Reynolds number ($δ^+$). Because the fluctuating pressure is predominantly a Poisson response to only two source terms -- a linear contribution from the mean shear coupled to a fluctuating velocity gradient, and a nonlinear contribution from the fluctuating velocity field -- the origin of this growth can be pinned down by elimination: if the linear source saturates at a Reynolds-number-independent value, the nonlinear source must carry the logarithmic growth. Here we supply the complementary evidence for inner-scaled invariance of the linear source at $δ^+$ up to $O(10^4)$, using the simultaneous velocity and velocity-gradient hot-wire measurements of Zimmermann \textit{et al.} (2019 \textit{JFM} vol. 869 pp. 182--213) acquired with a single eight-sensor probe in both a zero-pressure-gradient turbulent boundary layer and a high-Reynolds-number pipe flow. The inner-scaled factors entering the linear source collapse across Reynolds number, and the inertial-layer variance of the relevant fluctuating velocity gradient decays inversely with wall distance. Together with the established inner scaling of the mean shear, this is consistent with a linear wall-pressure contribution that, under inner normalisation, remains $O(1)$ as $δ^+\to\infty$. Both source terms then trace to one structural mechanism: the near-wall depletion of mean spanwise vorticity that caps the linear source also feeds, through vortex stretching, the inertial-layer fissures that carry the growing nonlinear contribution.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that the linear Poisson source for wall-pressure fluctuations stays inner-scaled and approximately constant at very high Reynolds number, so it cannot explain the observed logarithmic growth in wall-pressure variance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This isolates the growing wall-pressure variance to the nonlinear source, helping improve high-Reynolds-number turbulence models and wall-pressure predictions for aerodynamic and aeroacoustic design.
method: Used simultaneous velocity and velocity-gradient hot-wire measurements from Zimmermann et al. (2019).
Analyzed both a zero-pressure-gradient turbulent boundary layer and a high-Reynolds-number pipe flow.
Tested inner-scaling collapse of the factors entering the linear pressure source up to friction Reynolds numbers of order 10^4.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the linear-source factors collapse across Reynolds number and that the relevant inertial-layer velocity-gradient variance decays inversely with wall distance.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusion is based on indirect source-term separation from measured statistics, so extending it to other wall-bounded flows or even higher Reynolds numbers should be done cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: An Inner-Scaled Linear Contribution to Wall-Pressure Variance at High Reynolds Number

title: The PICNN-Assisted Physics-Preserving Scheme for Thermodynamically Consistent Two-Phase Flow in Porous Media
authors: Yuanshuo Kong, Xue Wang, Yujing Yan
abstract: In this paper, we develop a physics-informed convolutional neural network (PICNN) assisted physics-preserving method for a thermodynamically consistent model of incompressible and immiscible two-phase flow in porous media. Following the physics-preserving prediction-correction scheme of Li et al. \cite{li2025class}, the prediction step is performed by a PICNN trained with finite-volume residuals, where the interfacial fluxes are evaluated by the two-point flux approximation (TPFA) using two-point difference quotients of neighboring cell-centered unknowns to approximate interfacial normal gradients. The PICNN output is further corrected by a post-processing procedure to obtain energy-stable, mass-conservative, and bounds-preserving solutions. Numerical results show that the finite-volume residuals trained PICNN can replace the traditional prediction solver within the physics-preserving framework. Compared with conventional physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), the PICNN better captures local spatial interactions between each control volume and its neighboring cells, while the finite-volume residuals accommodate discontinuous permeability fields and interfacial flux continuity.

infographic.key_insight: A PICNN can replace the traditional prediction solver in a physics-preserving two-phase flow scheme while still yielding energy-stable, mass-conservative, and bounds-preserving solutions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical surrogate modeling strategy for porous-media flow simulation that is better suited than standard PINNs for local flux interactions and discontinuous permeability.
method: PICNN predicts the next-state solution using finite-volume residual training.
Interfacial fluxes are computed with TPFA and two-point difference quotients between neighboring cells.
A post-processing correction enforces thermodynamic consistency, mass conservation, and variable bounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical results showing that the finite-volume-residual-trained PICNN can successfully replace the conventional prediction solver within the physics-preserving framework.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the quality of the correction step and the ability of TPFA-based residuals to remain accurate on complex heterogeneous grids.
infographic.paper_title: The PICNN-Assisted Physics-Preserving Scheme for Thermodynamically Consistent Two-Phase Flow in Porous Media

title: Patagium and tail morphology shape aerodynamic performance and control authority in gliding-mammal-inspired wings
authors: Liming Zheng, Baihui Chen, Alexander van Zuijlen, Salua Hamaza
abstract: Gliding mammals exhibit diverse patagium and tail/uropatagium morphologies that may influence aerodynamic performance and maneuverability. Here, we use computational fluid dynamics to isolate the aerodynamic effects of representative gliding-mammal-inspired morphologies under controlled flow conditions. Three patagium configurations were compared to evaluate the effects of membrane outline on lift generation, drag, stall behavior and pitching moment. Three tail/uropatagium configurations were further tested under baseline, symmetric-deflection and asymmetric-deflection conditions to assess their longitudinal and lateral control authority. The results show that a broader patagium configuration generated the highest lift and lift coefficient, whereas an intermediate patagium morphology showed a smoother post-stall response with lower drag. For the tail configurations, the colugo-like integrated uropatagium enhanced lift and pitch-control authority under symmetric deflection, while the flat-tail configuration produced stronger rolling and yawing responses under asymmetric deflection. These findings indicate that gliding-mammal-inspired morphologies produce distinct aerodynamic trade-offs rather than a single optimal design. The results provide insight into the functional diversity of gliding mammal morphology and offer design guidance for bioinspired morphing aerial robots.

infographic.key_insight: Membrane shape and tail/uropatagium geometry create clear aerodynamic trade-offs in gliding-mammal-inspired wings, affecting lift, stall behavior, drag, and control authority.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results can guide the design of bioinspired morphing aerial robots by matching wing and tail morphology to the desired balance of efficiency, stability, and maneuverability.
method: Used computational fluid dynamics to isolate aerodynamic effects of representative gliding-mammal-inspired morphologies.
Compared three patagium configurations for lift, drag, stall, and pitching moment.
Tested three tail/uropatagium configurations under baseline, symmetric-deflection, and asymmetric-deflection conditions to assess longitudinal and lateral control authority.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparative CFD evaluation across multiple morphologies and deflection modes, with broader patagium giving the highest lift, intermediate shape giving smoother post-stall behavior, and different tail forms favoring pitch versus roll/yaw control.
infographic.watch_item: Results are based on controlled CFD conditions, so real-world performance may differ when structural flexibility, unsteady gusts, and full vehicle integration are included.
infographic.paper_title: Patagium and tail morphology shape aerodynamic performance and control authority in gliding-mammal-inspired wings

title: Direct numerical simulations of turbulent drag reduction via piezoelectric actuation
authors: Amir Amjadimanesh, Aman Kidanemariam, David Chappell, Mahdi Bodaghi, Amirreza Rouhi
abstract: We have conducted Direct Numerical Simulations of turbulent half-channel flow over realistic surface deformations at friction Reynolds number $Re_τ=200$. We generated the surface deformations using piezoelectric actuators. We simulated the piezoelectric actuation over the practical actuation frequency range $(119Hz\le f_\mathrm{act}\le543Hz)$ and voltage range $(250V\le Q \le500V)$ beneath an Aluminum sheet using Finite Element Analysis. The sheet deformation amplitude and actuation frequency in viscous units vary within the range $2 \le η^+_\mathrm{max} \le 34$, and $-0.58 \le ω^+ \le 0.70$. The vertical surface deformations from our actuation setup generate three types of waves: travelling, hybrid, and standing waves. Surface deformations are applied as bottom-wall boundary conditions of the turbulent channel flow to generate waves in the upstream, downstream, and spanwise directions. We achieved maximum drag reductions of 1.6\%, 5.4\%, and 27.6\% for upstream, downstream, and spanwise waves, respectively. The streamwise waves generate alternating adverse and favorable pressure gradients, which locally increase and decrease drag, leading to a marginal net change in drag. In contrast, spanwise waves introduce transverse shear, accompanied by high- and low-streamwise-momentum zones that respectively attenuate and energize the near-wall turbulence. Such disruption of the near-wall turbulence-regeneration cycle produces up to $27\%$ drag reduction for the realistic spanwise hybrid wave; such an outcome demonstrates the efficacy of unconventional realistic surface deformations in achieving significant drag reduction.

infographic.key_insight: Realistic piezoelectric surface deformations can generate wall waves that significantly alter near-wall turbulence, with spanwise waves delivering the strongest drag reduction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a practical route to passive/active hybrid drag-control surfaces for reducing skin-friction in turbulent channels and potentially improving fluid-transport efficiency.
method: Direct numerical simulations of turbulent half-channel flow at Re_tau=200.
Finite-element analysis of piezoelectric actuation beneath an aluminum sheet over 119–543 Hz and 250–500 V.
Applied resulting wall deformations as bottom-wall boundary conditions to test upstream, downstream, and spanwise wave effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study reports maximum drag reductions of 1.6% for upstream waves, 5.4% for downstream waves, and 27.6% for spanwise waves, with the strongest effect from the realistic spanwise hybrid wave.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is demonstrated at Re_tau=200 in DNS, so robustness, durability, and scalability to higher-Reynolds-number real flows and hardware constraints remain to be validated.
infographic.paper_title: Direct numerical simulations of turbulent drag reduction via piezoelectric actuation

title: Diffusiophoretic transport of colloids and emulsions in complex environments
authors: Amir A. Pahlavan
abstract: Chemical gradients are ubiquitous in porous and crowded environments, including soils, filters, fabrics, tissues, hydrogels, biofilms and living cells. They arise from displacement fronts, dissolution and precipitation, ion exchange, metabolism, root exudation, evaporation, gas dissolution, freeze--thaw cycles and externally imposed chemical treatments. These gradients can drive colloids, macromolecules and emulsion droplets by diffusiophoresis, while simultaneously driving diffusioosmotic flows along confining surfaces. Classical models of colloid transport in porous media emphasize hydrodynamic dispersion, surface interactions, straining, deposition, detachment and filtration. This chapter places diffusiophoresis within that broader transport framework and reviews how porous media generate, stretch, disperse and sustain the solute gradients that drive phoretic motion. We first discuss sources of chemical gradients and the distinction between spreading and mixing, then summarize classical colloid transport, the minimal physicochemical model for diffusiophoresis and diffusioosmosis, and the experimental platforms used to study these effects. Particular emphasis is placed on recent results showing that diffuse solute fronts can enhance phoretic removal from dead-end pores by prolonging the duration of forcing, and that cross-streamline migration within flowing pathways can change macroscopic breakthrough and dispersion by orders of magnitude. We close by discussing emulsion droplets, multiphase flows, confined and living media, and open problems, including the transition from algebraic mixing in two-dimensional micromodels to chaotic mixing in three-dimensional porous media.

infographic.key_insight: Chemical concentration gradients in porous and crowded media can actively move colloids and droplets via diffusiophoresis and diffusioosmosis, strongly altering transport beyond classical dispersion and filtration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for designing filters, soil remediation, tissue transport, hydrogel delivery, and microfluidic systems where chemical fronts can either enhance removal or dramatically change breakthrough.
method: Review of sources that generate and sustain solute gradients in complex media
Minimal physicochemical framework for diffusiophoresis and diffusioosmosis
Comparison with classical colloid-transport mechanisms and experimental platforms
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract synthesizes recent experimental findings showing that diffuse solute fronts can prolong phoretic forcing in dead-end pores and that cross-streamline migration can change breakthrough and dispersion by orders of magnitude.
infographic.watch_item: Effects depend strongly on gradient structure, pore geometry, and dimensionality, so results from 2D micromodels may not directly transfer to real 3D porous media.
infographic.paper_title: Diffusiophoretic transport of colloids and emulsions in complex environments

title: Mean-Flow Adjoint Sensitivity Analysis of Unsteady Flow Around Porous Cylinders Using a Homogenized Lattice Boltzmann Method
authors: Shota Ito, Johannes L. Grafen, Fedor Bukreev, Adrian Kummerländer, Mathias J. Krause
abstract: Adjoint-based sensitivity analysis is an indispensable tool for large-scale fluid-dynamic design and distributed control problems, yet its application to unsteady and turbulent flows is frequently hindered by the prohibitive memory footprint of transient checkpointing and the divergence of gradients in chaotic regimes. To address these computational bottlenecks, this paper presents a mean-flow adjoint sensitivity analysis framework for unsteady flows around porous cylinders using the homogenized lattice Boltzmann method (HLBM). Within this framework, solid structures are efficiently modeled as local porous media utilizing a Brinkman penalization approach. We systematically investigate HLBM-based adjoint gradients for drag and energy dissipation objective functionals, transitioning from steady laminar to unsteady, and finally to turbulent flow regimes. For the turbulent case at Re = 3900, a proof-of-concept is conducted where the framework relies on automatic differentiation to automatically generate adjoint kernels containing subgrid-scale (SGS) turbulence models for large eddy simulations (LES), circumventing manual derivation and allowing for a direct comparison against the frozen turbulence assumption (FTA).

infographic.key_insight: A mean-flow adjoint framework with homogenized lattice Boltzmann and Brinkman penalization enables practical sensitivity analysis for porous-cylinder flows from steady to turbulent regimes without relying on full transient checkpointing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a more tractable way to compute design gradients for drag and energy-dissipation optimization in complex fluid systems, especially when unsteady or turbulent dynamics make standard adjoints expensive or unstable.
method: Use HLBM to represent porous cylinders as locally homogenized porous media via Brinkman penalization.
Formulate a mean-flow adjoint to reduce memory burden and avoid gradient divergence in unsteady/chaotic flows.
Employ automatic differentiation to generate adjoint kernels with SGS LES terms and compare against frozen turbulence assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a systematic study spanning steady laminar, unsteady, and turbulent flow cases, including a proof-of-concept at Re = 3900.
infographic.watch_item: Mean-flow and frozen-turbulence approximations may limit gradient fidelity in strongly nonstationary turbulence, so validation against direct sensitivities or experiments is important.
infographic.paper_title: Mean-Flow Adjoint Sensitivity Analysis of Unsteady Flow Around Porous Cylinders Using a Homogenized Lattice Boltzmann Method

title: Comparative analysis of resistive immersed surface and immersed boundary methods for aortic valve simulation
authors: Han Zhao, Alexander D. Kaiser, Fanwei Kong, Aaron L. Brown, Zinan Hu, David Codoni
abstract: Numerical modeling of aortic valve dynamics is essential for understanding the complex fluid-structure interaction (FSI) governing valve biomechanics in health and disease. Immersed methods provide a flexible computational framework for simulating the large deformations of valve leaflets and associated blood flow without requiring body-fitted meshes. Among these approaches, the Resistive Immersed Surface (RIS) and Immersed Boundary (IB) methods are widely used. However, systematic comparative analysis of these methods for realistic aortic valve simulations has not been performed. In this work, we compare a prescribed-kinematics RIS workflow implemented in SimVascular's svMultiPhysics solver with a fully coupled IB workflow using IBAMR for trileaflet and bicuspid aortic valve configurations. The RIS method represents the valve as a surface with prescribed kinematics embedded in the fluid domain and introduces a penalty force that drives the surrounding fluid velocity toward the prescribed leaflet velocity. This formulation reduces modeling complexity and provides useful hemodynamic predictions when representative leaflet kinematics are available. In contrast, the IB method models the leaflets as elastic structures fully immersed in the fluid domain and resolves leaflet deformation through fully coupled two-way FSI. The study focuses on the extent to which RIS reproduces bulk hemodynamic features and transvalvular pressure gradients. Results show that the RIS method captures the large-scale flow structures and predicts the mean transvalvular pressure gradient with a relative error within 15% of the fully coupled IB simulation, improving to within 5% when inlet boundary conditions are matched, while reducing computational cost by approximately 60%.

infographic.key_insight: A prescribed-kinematics Resistive Immersed Surface (RIS) model can reproduce the main hemodynamic behavior of aortic valve flow nearly as well as a fully coupled Immersed Boundary (IB) model, but at much lower cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests RIS is a practical option for valve-flow studies when realistic leaflet motion is available and full fluid-structure coupling is not necessary.
method: RIS: prescribed leaflet kinematics embedded in the fluid with a penalty force to match fluid velocity to leaflet velocity.
IB: fully coupled two-way fluid-structure interaction with elastic leaflets resolved in the flow.
Comparison on trileaflet and bicuspid aortic valve simulations using SimVascular svMultiPhysics and IBAMR.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that RIS predicts the mean transvalvular pressure gradient within 15% of IB, improving to within 5% when inlet boundary conditions are matched, while reducing computational cost by about 60%.
infographic.watch_item: RIS depends on having representative prescribed leaflet kinematics, so accuracy may degrade if the motion or inlet conditions are not well matched.
infographic.paper_title: Comparative analysis of resistive immersed surface and immersed boundary methods for aortic valve simulation

title: Two-dimensional simulations of hydrodynamic spin coupling in a two-rotor corral
authors: Tsorng-Whay Pan, Jiwen He
abstract: We study hydrodynamic spin coupling in a two-rotor corral using DNS of 2D incompressible viscous fluid flow. An active rotor is driven at angular velocity W, and a nearby torque-free passive rotor selects an angular velocity w through hydrodynamic torque balance. The signed gear ratio Gamma=w/W distinguishes corotation from counterrotation, with Reynolds number Re=|Ω|r^2/ν. Motivated by a recent quasi-two-dimensional experiment, we use a DLM/FD method to compute planar phase diagrams of $Γ(G,Re)$ at corral sizes C=3, 4.5, and 6. The planar model recovers the benchmark gap route at Re=20: an intermediate counterrotation band, a wide-gap transition to corotation, gear-ratio magnitudes of order 10^{-2}, and the observed sequence of vortex attachment, detachment, and merger. It also produces a reentrant-like gap structure with a small-gap corotation region whose relation to the experimental close-range geometric state remains unresolved. The main discrepancy is the high-Re boundary. At the experimental mid-gap transect G about 0.3, the planar gear ratio approaches zero from the counterrotating side but does not cross through Re=400; at the narrower gap G=0.22, by contrast, the planar terminal spin reverses near Re=44. Wall-traction diagnostics show that this crossing is not the experimental shear-competition mechanism: the gap-facing counterrotating arc narrows but does not collapse or deflect as in the experiment, and the reversal at G=0.22 occurs by redistribution of the integrated planar torque. The strictly planar model therefore captures the broad gap-route architecture and the existence of a Reynolds-driven spin boundary, but displaces that boundary in gap and alters its surface-stress mechanism. The remaining mismatch points to finite-depth secondary motion, end-wall stresses, and apparatus geometry as plausible contributors to the experimental shear balance.

infographic.key_insight: 2D DNS shows that hydrodynamic spin coupling in a two-rotor corral follows the broad experimental gap-route pattern, but the Reynolds-number spin boundary is shifted and its mechanism differs from the experiment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results help predict when a passive rotor will corotate or counterrotate in confined viscous-flow devices, informing microfluidic rotors, mixers, and flow-driven gear-like systems.
method: 2D incompressible viscous DNS with a DLM/FD immersed-boundary style solver
Active rotor prescribed angular velocity; passive rotor determined by torque balance
Phase diagrams computed over gap ratio and Reynolds number for corral sizes C=3, 4.5, and 6
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports benchmark agreement at Re=20, including counterrotation-to-corotation gap transitions and vortex attachment/detachment/merger sequences, plus a reported reversal near Re=44 at G=0.22.
infographic.watch_item: A strictly planar model misses the experimental high-Re shear-competition mechanism, so finite-depth flow, end-wall stresses, and geometry effects may be essential for quantitative agreement.
infographic.paper_title: Two-dimensional simulations of hydrodynamic spin coupling in a two-rotor corral

title: Numerical Study of Compressibility and Velocity Parameter Effects on Spatially Evolving Supersonic Turbulent Shear Layers
authors: M. R. B. Shahadat, Z. Li, F. A. Jaberi, D. Livescu
abstract: Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) of a spatially developing supersonic turbulent shear layer are conducted for a range of convective Mach numbers ($M_c$) and velocity parameters ($λ$) to examine the effects of compressibility and advection on the growth rate, self-similarity, flow statistics, asymmetry, and entrainment of the layer. At distant downstream locations, self-similarity is attained for all cases. The self-similar region is identified by the collapse of normalized mean streamwise velocity, the constant peak of normalized Reynolds stresses, and the linear growth rate of the shear layer thickness and momentum thickness. Despite significant variations in lower-order and higher-order statistics across different $M_c$ and $λ$ values, profiles of all turbulence quantities examined collapse within the self-similar region using our proposed self-similar scalings. The self-similar forms of continuity, momentum, and energy equations have been formulated, incorporating compressibility and centerline shifts. The self-similar normalized density distribution inside the layer is used to explain the effects of compressibility on various flow statistics, including the far-field cross-stream velocity. The density variation is linked to dissipation effects as revealed by our analysis of the self-similar energy equation. An approximate equation for the cross-stream velocity is developed, and the profiles of cross-stream velocity obtained from this equation show good agreement with the DNS results. A geometric interpretation of the entrainment ratio is presented, and the approximate equation for the cross-stream velocity is used to provide a general closed-form expression of the entrainment ratio. The entrainment ratio increases with $M_c$ and $λ$, favoring excess entrainment on the high-speed side.

infographic.key_insight: Supersonic turbulent shear layers become self-similar far downstream, and their growth, asymmetry, and entrainment can be collapsed with compressibility-aware scalings that account for convective Mach number and velocity parameter effects.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results provide usable scaling laws and entrainment predictions for high-speed mixing layers, which are important for propulsion, combustion, and other compressible-flow system designs.
method: Direct Numerical Simulations of spatially developing supersonic turbulent shear layers.
Parametric study over multiple convective Mach numbers (Mc) and velocity parameters (λ).
Derivation of self-similar forms of continuity, momentum, and energy equations plus an approximate cross-stream velocity equation.
infographic.evidence_signal: DNS results show collapse of normalized velocity and turbulence profiles in the self-similar region, constant normalized Reynolds-stress peaks, and linear growth of shear-layer and momentum thickness.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed scalings and closed-form entrainment relation are validated within DNS cases studied here, so extrapolation to different geometries, Reynolds numbers, or strongly non-equilibrium flows should be done cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical Study of Compressibility and Velocity Parameter Effects on Spatially Evolving Supersonic Turbulent Shear Layers

title: Energy transfer, Intermittency and Mixing in Shear-Driven Stratified Turbulence
authors: Chandra Shekhar Lohani, Vishwanath Shukla
abstract: We investigate a stably stratified flow driven by deterministic Kolmogorov forcing that generates horizontal shear, using direct numerical simulations over a broad range of stratification strengths characterized by the Froude number $Fr$. As the stratification is progressively weakened, the flow exhibits a sequence of regimes: a buoyancy-dominated, strongly stratified regime, an intermediate regime characterized by Kelvin--Helmholtz instabilities and enhanced mixing, and a nearly isotropic turbulent regime. A key feature of the intermediate stratification range is the emergence of energetically significant vertically sheared horizontal flows (VSHFs), accompanied by a marked steepening of the reduced one-dimensional perpendicular kinetic energy spectra. The spectral energy transfer remains predominantly forward, although the perpendicular flux becomes negative at large horizontal scales; this apparent upscale transfer reflects anisotropic energy redistribution rather than a true inverse cascade. Strong stratification enhances intermittency, producing increasingly non-Gaussian vertical velocity fluctuations and large kurtosis associated with localized vertical bursts. The energetics-based mixing coefficient remains of order $10^{-1}$ over the parameter range investigated, with a modest enhancement near the Kelvin--Helmholtz instability regime.

infographic.key_insight: Weakening stratification drives the flow from buoyancy-dominated turbulence to Kelvin–Helmholtz-active mixing and then toward nearly isotropic turbulence, while intermediate stratification produces strong vertically sheared horizontal flows and steeper perpendicular spectra.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results help predict when shear-driven stratified flows will mix efficiently, develop intermittent bursts, or reorganize into anisotropic structures relevant to geophysical, atmospheric, and industrial mixing systems.
method: Direct numerical simulations of stably stratified Kolmogorov-forced shear flow
Parameter sweep over a broad range of Froude numbers to isolate stratification regimes
Spectral transfer, intermittency, and mixing diagnostics used to characterize energy pathways and flow structure
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports regime-dependent DNS results showing predominantly forward energy transfer, negative large-scale perpendicular flux from anisotropic redistribution, enhanced kurtosis under strong stratification, and a mixing coefficient remaining near 10^-1 with a modest peak near Kelvin–Helmholtz activity.
infographic.watch_item: The apparent upscale perpendicular flux should not be interpreted as a true inverse cascade, since it is attributed to anisotropic redistribution rather than net energy transfer to larger scales.
infographic.paper_title: Energy transfer, Intermittency and Mixing in Shear-Driven Stratified Turbulence

title: Influence of wind shear and veer on power, thrust, and induction of an actuator disk
authors: Kirby S. Heck, Storm A. Mata, Michael F. Howland
abstract: Wind shear and wind veer (gradients of wind speed and direction, respectively) are ubiquitous in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), and wind turbines therefore routinely operate in sheared and veered conditions. Previous field campaigns have observed statistically significant variations in power production efficiency (quantified by a power coefficient) upwards of 15% due to shear and veer. However, it is not yet clear how non-uniform inflow conditions alter rotor aerodynamics and drive these efficiency variations. In this study, we perform concurrent-precursor large-eddy simulations (LES) of an actuator disk-modeled wind turbine across stratified ABL conditions to demonstrate that shear and veer can reduce wind power efficiency by more than 20%. To support these ABL simulations, we perform simplified inflow LES where shear and veer are controlled independently. Using these controlled simulations, we demonstrate that shear and veer effects can be decomposed into: (1) geometric effects, due to changes in rotor-equivalent wind speed, and (2) inductive effects, which change the rotor aerodynamics and induced velocities. Inductive effects of wind shear modulate the power coefficient through changes to the local induction, while inductive effects of wind veer reduce the power coefficient by generating an adverse pressure gradient at the rotor scale. The geometric and inductive effects of shear and veer approximately linearly superimpose, with increasing losses as shear and veer magnitudes increase. Inductive effects account for a significant fraction of the observed losses, and the induction of a turbine is affected by shear, veer, and wall proximity through processes that are neglected in existing engineering models. Revealing the mechanisms through which shear and veer affect rotor performance establishes a framework that can enable improved power prediction in realistic ABL conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Wind shear and veer can cut actuator-disk power efficiency by more than 20% because they change both the incoming wind geometry and the rotor’s induction aerodynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Wind-turbine power prediction models should account for shear- and veer-driven induction effects, not just rotor-equivalent wind speed, to better estimate performance in realistic atmospheric boundary layers.
method: Concurrent-precursor LES of an actuator disk turbine in stratified atmospheric boundary layers
Controlled inflow LES with shear and veer varied independently
Decomposition of losses into geometric and inductive contributions
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports LES results showing statistically meaningful efficiency changes, with shear and veer together reducing power coefficient by more than 20% and each effect approximately linearly superimposing.
infographic.watch_item: The findings are based on actuator-disk LES and simplified inflow controls, so translation to fully resolved turbine blades and diverse site conditions may require additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Influence of wind shear and veer on power, thrust, and induction of an actuator disk

title: Fourier Neural Operators for Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
authors: Chelsea Maria John, Thibaut Lunet, Sebastian Götschel, Andreas Herten, Stefan Kesselheim, Daniel Ruprecht
abstract: We propose an improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for modeling two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection by predicting time increments instead of full solutions, achieving higher accuracy than a standard FNO baseline. The resulting model is compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms inference), while maintaining similar accuracy as demonstrated in previous benchmarks. We show that although FNOs generalize to finer meshes, accuracy remains limited by the resolution of the training data.

infographic.key_insight: Predicting time increments with an improved Fourier Neural Operator yields a more accurate and compact surrogate for 2D Rayleigh-Bénard convection than a standard full-solution FNO.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables fast, low-memory CFD surrogates for convection-driven flows, supporting rapid simulation, screening, and reduced-cost modeling workflows.
method: Use a Fourier Neural Operator to learn the convection dynamics in spectral space.
Predict the next time increment rather than the entire state to improve accuracy.
Benchmark against a standard FNO baseline on 2D Rayleigh-Bénard convection.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model is reported at 314k parameters, 1.26 MB, and 7 ms inference while maintaining similar benchmark accuracy to prior results.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to finer meshes is possible, but accuracy is still constrained by the resolution of the training data.
infographic.paper_title: Fourier Neural Operators for Rayleigh-Bénard Convection

title: Effect of surfactant kinetics on the wetting following the drop impact onto rough surfaces
authors: S. Rodríguez-Aparicio, M. Herreruela-Rosado, M. G. Cabezas, J. M. Montanero, E. J. Vega
abstract: We experimentally analyze the effect of a surfactant on wetting following drop impact on rough surfaces, paying special attention to the role of dynamic surface tension. To this end, we compare the results obtained with Triton X-100, SDS, and Surfynol 465. For concentrations below the critical micelle concentration $c_{\textin{cmc}}$, the evolution of the coverage area is nearly identical for all three surfactants, suggesting that the surfactant concentration is too low to significantly influence droplet spreading. In contrast, pronounced differences emerge due to the distinct dynamic surface tensions of the surfactants at $c/c_{\textin{cmc}}=2$. The evolution of the coverage area during spreading is nearly the same for pure water droplets and those containing Surfynol 465, indicating that surfactant depletion is negligible during the rapid spreading stage. As the Weber number increases, droplet spreading becomes progressively less sensitive to surface tension, thereby reducing the influence of surfactant adsorption kinetics. Nevertheless, Surfynol 465 produces larger coverage areas than Triton X-100 and SDS. The final coverage area is governed by the quasi-static recession of the triple contact line, which is controlled by the receding contact angle. Surfynol 465 consistently yields substantially larger final coverage areas across the range of surface roughness considered in this study.

infographic.key_insight: Surfactant kinetics matter mainly when dynamic surface tension stays high during impact; at low concentrations or high Weber number, wetting becomes much less sensitive to surfactant type.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For rough-surface coating, spray, and contamination-control applications, choosing a surfactant with favorable adsorption dynamics can significantly increase final coverage and improve wetting performance.
method: Drop-impact experiments on rough surfaces
Compared Triton X-100, SDS, and Surfynol 465
Varied surfactant concentration, Weber number, and surface roughness
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports nearly identical coverage evolution below CMC, strong differences at 2×CMC due to dynamic surface tension, and consistently larger final coverage for Surfynol 465.
infographic.watch_item: The findings are experimental and specific to the tested rough surfaces and surfactants, so transfer to other chemistries or texture scales may require revalidation.
infographic.paper_title: Effect of surfactant kinetics on the wetting following the drop impact onto rough surfaces

title: No evidence of vorticity production from initially irrotational turbulent gravitational collapse
authors: Axel Brandenburg, Evangelia Ntormousi, Jennifer Schober
abstract: Gravitational collapse creates large amounts of kinetic energy that could potentially seed turbulence. If such turbulence were also suitable to initiate dynamo action, the resulting magnetic field would further modify the dynamics, especially on small length scales. However, a small-scale dynamo requires vortical turbulence, while the collapse produces mainly irrotational motions, which may not be efficient for dynamo action. Here, we study the efficiency of vorticity production during a turbulent collapse. We use a barotropic equation of state, where pressure and density gradients are parallel, and no magnetic field, so that vorticity can only be produced by viscosity. Using direct numerical simulations of gravitational collapse, we show that, for the parameter space accessible to our numerical resolution, this effect is related to the initial irrotational turbulence and is not a consequence of the collapse flow.

infographic.key_insight: In barotropic, non-magnetic gravitational collapse, the collapse itself does not generate significant new vorticity; the observed vorticity is tied to the initially irrotational turbulent state and viscous effects.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests that collapse-driven flows may be poor candidates for small-scale dynamo initiation unless additional physics or mechanisms create sustained vortical turbulence.
method: Direct numerical simulations of turbulent gravitational collapse
Barotropic equation of state to suppress baroclinic vorticity generation
No magnetic field, so vorticity production can only arise from viscosity
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the numerically accessible parameter space, the simulations indicate that vorticity production is linked to the initial irrotational turbulence rather than to the collapse flow itself.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusion is limited to the resolution and parameter range of the simulations, so unresolved small-scale effects could still alter vorticity generation.
infographic.paper_title: No evidence of vorticity production from initially irrotational turbulent gravitational collapse

title: Visualizing Lagrangian Heat Transport Paths and Density Structures in Unsteady Heat Transfer
authors: Besm Osman, Andrei Jalba, Michel Speetjens, Anna Vilanova
abstract: Convective heat transfer is traditionally visualized from a Eulerian perspective using scalar temperature fields, offering limited insight into the underlying transport mechanisms. A Lagrangian view, analogous to mass transport along fluid paths, can reveal coherent structures and transport routes invisible from a Eulerian view of temperature. However, heat transport is aperiodic and non-conservative, hampering the application of fluid mixing and transport visualization techniques, developed primarily for time-periodic, conservative transport. We present a particle-based visualization technique that addresses these challenges by advecting massless particles along a time-reparameterized spacetime formulation of thermal transport, accumulating path contributions to reveal coherent transport routes and finite-time attracting and repelling structures that conventional methods cannot show.

infographic.key_insight: The paper reframes unsteady heat transfer as a Lagrangian transport problem, using advected particles to expose coherent heat pathways and finite-time attracting/repelling structures hidden by standard temperature plots.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This can improve diagnosis and design of thermal systems by revealing where heat actually travels, not just where temperature is high or low.
method: Advect massless particles through a time-reparameterized spacetime formulation of thermal transport.
Accumulate particle path contributions to visualize coherent transport routes.
Extract finite-time attracting and repelling structures from the resulting Lagrangian field.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract claims the method reveals transport routes and finite-time structures that conventional Eulerian temperature visualizations cannot show.
infographic.watch_item: Because heat transport is aperiodic and non-conservative, the approach may be sensitive to trajectory integration and time-reparameterization choices.
infographic.paper_title: Visualizing Lagrangian Heat Transport Paths and Density Structures in Unsteady Heat Transfer

title: GQL-Based Physical-Constraint-Preserving High-Order Finite Difference Schemes for Special Relativistic Hydrodynamics in Arbitrary Dimensions
authors: Linfeng Xu, Shengrong Ding, Kailiang Wu
abstract: High-order accurate simulations of special relativistic hydrodynamics (RHD) are prone to numerical breakdown if intrinsic physical constraints (positive rest-mass density/pressure and subluminal velocity) are violated near strong discontinuities. In this work, we develop a robust and efficient physical-constraint-preserving (PCP) flux-limiting framework for high-order schemes, using finite-difference WENO as a representative example. By leveraging the geometric quasilinearization (GQL) representation, which equivalently reformulates the nonlinear RHD constraints into a family of linear inequalities, we integrate a Zalesak-type Flux-Corrected Transport (FCT) update into a scalar-style limiter that acts directly on conservative variables. A critical innovation is the explicit, non-iterative determination of limiting parameters via a rational stereographic parameterization of the GQL normal vector. This technique transforms the required worst-case minimization over auxiliary variables into a generalized Rayleigh-quotient formulation, allowing the optimal parameters to be obtained by solving small symmetric eigenvalue problems ($2\times2$ in 1D; $(d+1)\times(d+1)$ in $d$ dimensions). Relaxed variants are further introduced to reduce computational costs in multidimensions while retaining the PCP guarantee. Extensive numerical benchmarks ranging from 1D to 3D, including ultra-relativistic Riemann problems and astrophysical jets, demonstrate that the proposed method robustly enforces physical admissibility, sharply resolves discontinuities, and maintains design-order accuracy for smooth solutions.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a physical-constraint-preserving limiter for high-order relativistic hydrodynamics that enforces positive density/pressure and subluminal velocity by turning nonlinear admissibility conditions into small eigenvalue problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a robust way to run high-order shock-capturing simulations in special relativistic flows without numerical breakdown near strong discontinuities.
method: Uses a GQL reformulation to convert relativistic physical constraints into linear inequalities.
Adds a Zalesak-type flux-corrected transport update to finite-difference WENO schemes.
Computes optimal limiter parameters non-iteratively via stereographic parameterization and small symmetric eigenproblems.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive tests from 1D to 3D, including ultra-relativistic Riemann problems and astrophysical jets, showing stable constraint enforcement and design-order accuracy on smooth solutions.
infographic.watch_item: The multidimensional relaxation variants reduce cost, but practical efficiency and implementation complexity may still depend on repeatedly solving small eigenproblems and integrating the limiter into existing codes.
infographic.paper_title: GQL-Based Physical-Constraint-Preserving High-Order Finite Difference Schemes for Special Relativistic Hydrodynamics in Arbitrary Dimensions

title: Lock-exchange flow regimes under low air Froude number bubble curtains
authors: Shravan K. R. Raaghav, Herman J. H. Clercx, Matias Duran-Matute
abstract: The flow and density field characteristics around a bubble curtain in a laboratory scale lock-exchange setup are investigated using two-phase large-eddy simulations. We study the detailed hydrodynamics and show that there are three qualitatively distinct (sub)regimes within the previously classified breakthrough regime. The occurrence of these regimes depends not only on air Froude number that characterises the relative strength of the bubble curtain and the gravity current, but also on an additional non-dimensional parameter: the density ratio between the salt and fresh water. The dependence on this additional parameter is also observed in how effective bubble curtains are in blocking the transport of salt to the fresh part of the lock. Hence, it has important implications for the optimisation of bubble curtains in ship locks.

infographic.key_insight: Two-phase LES reveals that the bubble-curtain “breakthrough” regime actually splits into three distinct subregimes, governed by both air Froude number and salt-to-freshwater density ratio.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Bubble-curtain performance in ship locks cannot be optimized using air Froude number alone; the density ratio also strongly affects salt transport blocking efficiency.
method: Two-phase large-eddy simulations of a laboratory lock-exchange setup
Detailed analysis of flow and density fields around a bubble curtain
Regime identification across varying air Froude number and salt-freshwater density ratio
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports simulation-based hydrodynamic and transport results showing three subregimes and differing salt-blocking effectiveness across parameter variations.
infographic.watch_item: Results are based on laboratory-scale simulations, so scale-up to full ship-lock operations may require additional validation under real operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Lock-exchange flow regimes under low air Froude number bubble curtains

title: Plant-On-a-Disc (POD): A Phytofluidic platform enabling In Situ Root Analysis
authors: Kaushal Agarwal, Sumit Kumar Mehta, Pranab Kumar Mondal
abstract: Phytofluidic platforms have enabled controlled studies of plant roots, however, most existing systems either impose geometric confinement without flow or introduce hydrodynamics in single-channel devices that limit throughput and disrupt downstream analysis. New experimental platforms are therefore needed to investigate how roots integrate mechanical confinement and hydrodynamic nutrient transport, two defining features of the rhizosphere that remain difficult to reproduce under controlled laboratory conditions. Here, we present the Plant-on-a-Disc (POD), a phytofluidic platform that enables the parallel cultivation of eight seedlings under controlled hydrodynamic conditions while allowing non-invasive, in situ multimodal analysis of the intact root-shoot system. The device is fabricated in PDMS using a cost-effective wire-drawing technique to generate radial microchannels that converge into a central sump beneath an optical window. This design enables sequential bright-field, fluorescence, and Raman measurements using a single microscope objective without disturbing neighbouring seedlings. Dimensionless transport analysis and finite-element modelling confirm that the radial architecture equalizes hydraulic resistance across channels, establishing creeping laminar flow with convection-dominated nutrient transport under physiologically safe shear conditions. Using Brassica seedlings, we show that hydrodynamic flow drives coordinated root responses across multiple scales. Roots grown in flow condition exhibit accelerated elongation, substantial ROS generation and anisotropic cortical cell expansion, accompanied by carotenoid signatures detected by Raman spectroscopy.

infographic.key_insight: Plant-on-a-Disc (POD) combines parallel root cultivation with controlled radial microflow, enabling non-invasive in situ study of how hydrodynamics and confinement jointly shape root behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The POD architecture offers a low-cost, scalable phytofluidic platform for reproducible root phenotyping under physiologically relevant flow with minimal disturbance to adjacent samples.
method: PDMS device fabricated with a wire-drawing process to create radial microchannels feeding a central sump under an optical window.
Eight seedlings are cultured in parallel while bright-field, fluorescence, and Raman measurements are taken sequentially with one microscope objective.
Dimensionless transport analysis and finite-element modeling were used to verify balanced hydraulic resistance, creeping laminar flow, and convection-dominated transport.
infographic.evidence_signal: In Brassica seedlings, flow conditions produced faster root elongation, strong ROS accumulation, anisotropic cortical cell expansion, and Raman-detectable carotenoid signatures.
infographic.watch_item: The platform’s utility depends on maintaining uniform low-shear flow and precise alignment for multimodal optical access, which may be sensitive to fabrication variability.
infographic.paper_title: Plant-On-a-Disc (POD): A Phytofluidic platform enabling In Situ Root Analysis

title: Pressure-drop localization and momentum insulation in liquid-gas coexistence Poiseuille flow
authors: Naoko Nakagawa, Shin-ichi Sasa
abstract: We study pressure-driven Poiseuille flow of a one-component fluid between adiabatic plates in liquid-gas coexistence. The analysis uses Poiseuille flow and Fourier heat conduction in the bulk regions together with particle and energy conservation. From these bulk equations, we identify extremely small dimensionless parameters $A^\mathrm{L}$ and $A^\mathrm{G}$ describing coexistence Poiseuille flow, whose smallness comes from squared microscopic-to-macroscopic length ratios. In weak driving with macroscopic liquid and gas regions, the pressure difference is concentrated across the interfacial region, and the ordinary Poiseuille particle current is strongly reduced. For equal-temperature reservoirs, this residual particle current produces interfacial cooling.

infographic.key_insight: In liquid-gas coexistence Poiseuille flow, almost all of the pressure drop localizes at the interface, which strongly suppresses the usual bulk momentum-driven particle current.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests that multiphase microfluidic and thermal systems can exhibit strong flow resistance and interfacial cooling even under weak driving, so interface effects must be included in design models.
method: Combine Poiseuille flow relations in the liquid and gas bulk regions with Fourier heat conduction.
Enforce particle conservation and energy conservation across the coexistence flow.
Derive small dimensionless parameters A^L and A^G from microscopic-to-macroscopic length-scale ratios.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper’s conclusion is based on analytical bulk equations and scaling arguments, showing that in the weak-driving limit with macroscopic liquid and gas regions the pressure difference concentrates at the interface.
infographic.watch_item: The result relies on continuum bulk theory and very small scale-separation parameters, so its applicability may be limited when interface thickness or microscopic effects are not negligible.
infographic.paper_title: Pressure-drop localization and momentum insulation in liquid-gas coexistence Poiseuille flow
